evidence.claim: Lumber and salt fortunes built a neighborhood along Center Avenue.
evidence.quote: Wealthy families, mostly in the lumber and salt trade, found that the area was convenient to bay City's commercial district, while still maintaining a quiet residential feel.

evidence.claim: Center Avenue carries M-25 through Bay City’s historic residential neighborhood, where Italianate, Queen Anne and Châteauesque houses stand among later architectural styles.
evidence.quote: These including some of the finest Victorian Italianate, Stick style, Queen Anne, Richardsonian Romanesque, and Châteauesque buildings in the city.

evidence.claim: Center Avenue carries M-25 through Bay City’s historic residential neighborhood, where Italianate, Queen Anne and Châteauesque houses stand among later architectural styles.
evidence.quote: for the section of M-25 along Center Avenue between Madison Avenue and the eastern city limits.

evidence.claim: Michigan’s Department of Transportation designated the stretch from Madison Avenue to the eastern city limits a historic heritage route in 1997, now a Pure Michigan Historic Byway.
evidence.quote: The section of M-25 in the City of Bay City was named what is now called a Pure Michigan Historic Byway by the Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT). This designation was created on October 23, 1997, for the section of M-25 along Center Avenue between Madison Avenue and the eastern city limits.

evidence.claim: The avenue had been platted in 1837, but its residential development came in the 1870s and 1880s.
evidence.quote: Although the area had first been platted in 1837, development did not occur until the 1870s and 1880s.

evidence.claim: Bay City’s growth created a housing shortage, and wealthy lumber and salt families chose this neighborhood near the commercial district.
evidence.quote: The influx of people created a housing shortage for rich and poor alike, and wealthy citizens chose to build along Center Avenue.

evidence.claim: Bay City’s growth created a housing shortage, and wealthy lumber and salt families chose this neighborhood near the commercial district.
evidence.quote: Wealthy families, mostly in the lumber and salt trade, found that the area was convenient to bay City's commercial district, while still maintaining a quiet residential feel.

evidence.claim: When lumbering declined after the turn of the century, agriculture, iron and textiles took its place.
evidence.quote: After the turn of the century, lumbering went into decline, and new industry and trades took its place, including agriculture, iron, and textiles.

evidence.claim: Newly wealthy businessmen built among the earlier houses and farther east; development continued until the Great Depression.
evidence.quote: Newer wealthy businessmen followed their predecessors and built houses along Center Avenue, both in among the earlier houses and farther eastward. The district continued to expand until the Great Depression.

evidence.claim: Preservation became a neighborhood effort in 2005, when residents began meeting and formed the Center Avenue Neighborhood Association. The association later helped the city administer a National Scenic Byways grant.
evidence.quote: In 2005, a group of neighbors began meeting in the area to promote historical preservation in the neighborhood. From this, the Center Avenue Neighborhood Association (CANA) was born. The Association has helped promote the neighborhood and support the City of Bay City in the administration of a National Scenic Byways grant.

evidence.claim: The neighborhood developed in the 1870s and 1880s, attracting wealthy families from the lumber and salt trades to an address near Bay City’s commercial district.
evidence.quote: Although the area had first been platted in 1837, development did not occur until the 1870s and 1880s. Wealthy families, mostly in the lumber and salt trade, found that the area was convenient to bay City's commercial district, while still maintaining a quiet residential feel.

evidence.claim: The neighborhood has retained the residences and streetscapes that first made it a fashionable address.
evidence.quote: In the subsequent years, the district has maintained the residences and streetscapes that made it a fashionable place to build early in its history.

evidence.claim: Two elaborate porches distinguish the Frederick Bradley residence at 1400 Center Avenue.
evidence.quote: Frederick Bradley Residence - 1400 Center Avenue. A massive Queen Anne home with a complexly asymmetrical floorplan and massing and two elaborate porches, constructed in 1887-89.

evidence.claim: Built from 1887 to 1889, the large Queen Anne house has an asymmetrical arrangement of rooms and building volumes.
evidence.quote: A massive Queen Anne home with a complexly asymmetrical floorplan and massing and two elaborate porches, constructed in 1887-89.

evidence.claim: Its construction fell within the neighborhood’s nineteenth-century building period, before later houses introduced Prairie, Arts and Crafts and other twentieth-century styles.
evidence.quote: Later residences from the first three decades of the 20th century include Georgian Revival, Renaissance Revival, Gothic Revival, Prairie Style, Arts and Crafts, and Bungalow structures.

evidence.claim: The district’s original Center Avenue section and portions of Fifth and Sixth Avenues entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1982; its boundaries expanded in 2012.
evidence.quote: The original section, along Center and portions of Fifth and Sixth, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. A boundary increase including the other sections of the neighborhood was listed in 2012.
